payload.body: Contact quotient (Cn) is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the fraction of the fundamental period T0 during which the vocal folds are in contact in voiced phonation. From the electroglottographic signal (EGG) or glottal-flow waveform g(n), the contact phase is the interval during which the signal indicates vocal fold contact, and Cn = contact phase / T0. Parameters: (1) the electroglottographic or glottal-flow signal estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the contact-phase extraction method (EGG derivative zero crossings or glottal-flow extrema). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; the maintained reference range for typical phonation sits near 0.5-0.7, and an elevated contact quotient indicates prolonged vocal fold contact as in pressed or hypofunctional phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software (Praat, laryngology suites) from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. payload.body: Period perturbation is a class of voice-quality parameters that quantify the cycle-to-cycle variation in the fundamental period of voiced speech. The general measure computes the normalized difference between consecutive periods: given N consecutive glottal cycles with periods P_i, perturbation = normalized deviation of |P_{i+1} - P_i| relative to the mean period. Named variants include: APQ1 (average absolute difference quotient), JRR (jitter ratio), and JDP (jitter absolute difference). Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal, (2) the pitch-synchronous segmentation at cycle boundaries, (3) the specific perturbation variant formula. Reported in percent or absolute units (ms). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a measurement class by the discipline of laryngology and speech science; implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), taught in voice-disorder curricula, and standardized in clinical practice. [formal: perturbatio periodica | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

Parameters: (1) the voiced speech signal, (2) the pitch-synchronous segmentation at cycle boundaries, (3) the specific perturbation variant formula. Reported in percent or absolute units (ms). Persistence mechanism: maintained as a measurement class by the discipline of laryngology and speech science; implemented in voice-analysis toolkits (Praat, laryngology suites), taught in voice-disorder curricula, and standardized in clinical practice. payload.body: source-filter-separation is a human-made signal processing technique that decomposes an observed signal into two additive or convolutive components: a source (excitation) component representing the energy origin, and a filter (resonance) component representing the shaping mechanism. The technique operates by applying one of several decomposition methods — (1) inverse filtering, where the estimated transfer function H(z) is inverted to recover e(n) = x(n) * H_inv(z), (2) deconvolution, where the source is recovered by frequency-domain division of the spectrum by the filter spectrum, or (3) cepstral analysis, where the logarithm of the spectrum separates slowly-varying filter envelope from rapidly-varying source structure. Parameters: (1) the input signal x(n), (2) the source-filter model assumptions (convolutive vs additive), (3) the decomposition method and its parameters. The persistence mechanism is algorithmic implementation in DSP software (Praat, MATLAB, Kaldi), documentation in signal processing textbooks (Rabiner and Schafer, Oppenheim and Schafer), and standardized use in speech analysis, audio processing, and system identification pipelines. payload.body: The asymmetry coefficient is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the asymmetry of the glottal airflow pulse in voiced phonation. It measures the degree to which the glottal flow pulse is skewed toward the open or close phase of the glottal cycle. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the asymmetry coefficient is computed as the ratio of the open-phase duration to the close-phase duration within the period, or equivalently as the skewness of the flow pulse. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the asymmetry computation method (open-phase/close-phase ratio or flow-pulse skewness). It is reported as a dimensionless ratio; a value of 1 indicates symmetric phonation, while values deviating from 1 indicate pressed (value above 1) or breathy (value below 1) phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map. [formal: coefficient asymmetricus | substrate: mind | horizon: a moment | explicit: yes | epoch: 0.02]

payload.body: The return phase is a voice-quality parameter quantifying the return phase of the glottal airflow pulse in voiced phonation. It measures the timing of the return of the glottal flow to its baseline after the excitation pulse, characterizing the decay characteristics of the glottal source. Given the glottal-flow waveform g(n) and the fundamental period T0, the return phase is computed as the time from the flow maximum to the return of the flow to baseline within the period. Parameters: (1) the glottal-flow waveform estimated per voiced frame, (2) the fundamental period T0 from pitch tracking, (3) the return-phase extraction method (time from flow maximum to baseline return). It is reported in milliseconds or as a fraction of the fundamental period; the maintained reference range for typical phonation is within the normal glottal cycle timing, and deviations indicate glottal source abnormalities such as pressed or breathy phonation. Persistence mechanism: the standardized clinical voice-quality parameter computed by voice-analysis software from the glottogram, taught in voice-disorder curricula, and revised as the standard; it persists as a maintained member of the voice-quality measurement map.
